title: The son who stayed (Luke 15:25–32)
hook: the older brother won't go into the party, and the father comes out to him too

segments.voice: Yesterday, the son who left, who had lived riotously, came home, and the father ran down the road. Your line was the father runs. But there's another son.

The older son has been out in the field all day, working, like every day. As he comes near the house, he hears music. Dancing. He calls a servant over: what's going on? And the servant tells him, happily: your brother's come home, and your father has killed the fatted calf, because he's got him back safe and sound. The older son stops in the yard. He won't go in. It's the spot where the dutiful one stands, listening to someone else's party.
screen: `A LONG DAY IN THE FIELD.` → `MUSIC FROM THE HOUSE.` → `HE WON'T GO IN.`

segments.voice: The father comes out. He ran down the road for the younger son, and now he leaves his own party to plead with the older one. Luke says he began to entreat him. And the older son lets it all out. All these years I've served you. I never once disobeyed. And you never gave me so much as a young goat to celebrate with my friends. But when "this thy son" comes back, who wasted your money, you kill the fatted calf for him. This thy son. Not my brother. He doesn't say the word. The father answers with a word of great tenderness. In the Douay-Rheims: "Son, thou art always with me, and all I have is thine." The Greek word is teknon, child. Not a scolding. My child, you've been with me all along. Everything I have is yours. Some readers hear in it: you never had to earn it. Then the father gives the word back to him. It was right to celebrate, he says, because "this thy brother" was dead, and is alive again; was lost, and is found. Your son, says the older boy. Your brother, says the father. And then the story stops. We never find out whether the older son goes in. Jesus leaves the door open. He was telling this story to people grumbling that he ate with sinners, and the ending is left for them to write, and for anyone listening. Some Catholics pray with Rembrandt's painting of this parable, where the older son stands off to the side, watching.
screen: `THE FATHER COMES OUT AGAIN.` · `THIS THY SON, NOT MY BROTHER.` · `TEKNON — MY CHILD.` · `THE STORY STOPS AT THE DOOR.` · then, large: `ALL I HAVE IS THINE.`

segments.voice: Is there someone you're keeping score with, someone who got the thing you worked for, or got forgiven too easily? Let the feeling come up, name it, resentment, and notice where it sits in your body, without arguing with it or feeding it more reasons; then let the father's words sit next to it: all I have is yours. If you pray, you can hand God the scorecard.
teknon. The tender Greek word, child, the father used for his angry older son, who wouldn't go in to the party.
Your line: all I have is yours. The door to the party is still open. Forty-eight days, and counting.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the whole parable of the prodigal son, older brother included, in Lent, and some use it to examine their consciences before confession, asking which son they resemble.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 15:31 and the phrases 'this thy son' (15:30), 'this thy brother' (15:32) given from memory; confirm.
Greek τέκνον in Luke 15:31 (the Douay-Rheims and KJV say 'Son'); confirm.
The carry 'all I have is yours' is a modern rendering; the Douay-Rheims 'all I have is thine' is quoted in the teach.

Rembrandt, The Return of the Prodigal Son (c. 1668, Hermitage); the standing figure at right is commonly identified as the older son. Mentioned as something many Catholics pray with (Henri Nouwen's book popularized this); confirm.
